extracted.intended_audience: policy makers, regulators, civil society organisations, and researchers assessing public consultations in India
extracted.subtask_description: A methodology for evaluating the procedural integrity and quality of pre-legislative/public consultations (draft laws and regulations), focused on Indian Central/State governments and regulatory bodies but informed by international best practices. The page describes a 10-criterion scorecard grouped under four overarching metrics and gives scoring guidance and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the consultation document clearly articulate the rationale behind the proposed policy or legal change: is the problem defined well, with relevant background, existing issues, and the objectives it aims to achieve? A strong justification helps citizens understand the 'why' behind the proposal, enabling more informed and relevant feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess qualitatively whether the consultation document explains why the proposal is needed and the context for it. This criterion is borrowed from Section 2 of the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy (PLCP), which states departments should publish a brief justification, essential elements, broad financial implications, and estimated assessment of impacts (environment, rights, livelihoods, etc.). The jury has retained this criterion across editions as originally conceived. Example: scored 5/5 where sections thoroughly state need and objectives (as in Draft Kerala IT Policy 2023 Sections 1.1 and 2.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the proposed changes, new provisions, or key components of the draft are clearly outlined so citizens can identify and understand exactly what is being proposed and its key features (proposals, key rights and penalties, or other government interventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative test: can an average reader discern the proposals with no room for ambiguity. Drawn from PLCP guidance that essential elements of the proposed legislation be placed in the public domain. Example: the Draft Kerala IT Policy's 'Policy Framework' chapter scored highly when it laid down directions for growth, enablers, outcomes, and addressed issues like information security and infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the potential impact of the proposed draft—including financial, social, and environmental impacts—been analysed and stated within the document? Transparency about positive and negative impacts is crucial for informed feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally evaluated subjectively across financial, social and economic impacts; later refined to increase granularity. For the second edition the criterion was refined with support from Trustbridge Foundation and Dr. Renuka Sane into a set of 25 sub-questions whose answers feed the overall score. Assessment should consider cost-benefit analysis, alternative strategies, timelines for implementation, environmental impacts, long-term evaluation, and rural integration. Example: Draft Kerala IT Policy was penalised for missing explicit cost-benefit analysis and clear timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Can an average reader, without specialised domain expertise, easily understand the draft? This evaluates readability, clarity of language, avoidance of jargon or provision of explanations for technical terms, and user-friendliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative assessment of document readability and structure. The PLCP (Section 5) recommends that every draft be accompanied by an explanatory note in simple language. Look for plain-language drafting, clear explanations of technical concepts, and presence of summaries or visual aids. Example: absence of visual aids or summaries can lower score even if structure and clarity are otherwise good (Draft Kerala IT Policy lost a point for lacking visual summaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a consultation is open for a reasonable period that allows stakeholders to review the document, understand implications, and prepare feedback. Insufficient duration limits participation and quality of responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from PLCP Section 2 which suggests a minimum period of thirty days. Scoring history: Edition one used a sliding 1–5 scale by days open ( <20 days =1; 20–29 days=2; 30 days exactly=3; 30–59 days=4; 60+ days=5). For the second edition the jury moved to a binary quantitative scoring to align with the PLCP: score 1 for consultations under 30 days, score 5 for consultations 30 days or longer (binary 1 or 5 chosen to keep scale compatibility). Example: Draft Kerala IT Policy scored 5/5 with a 96-day period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether outreach was comprehensive and diverse across media and channels to ensure the consultation reached a broad range of relevant stakeholders and the general public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from PLCP Section 3 which recommends publicity via print/electronic media as needed to reach affected people. Evaluate active dissemination beyond mere publication on a government website—social media, print, community forums, targeted invitations, and compilations of outreach efforts. Scoring is based on documented outreach activities (e.g., social posts across platforms, targeted communications). Example: Draft Kerala IT Policy received 4/5 for extensive social media and website dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback Collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether multiple, accessible avenues were provided for stakeholders to submit responses (online portals, email, post, public hearings, interviews), ensuring participation regardless of digital literacy or access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builds on OECD Practitioner's Guide which recommends evaluating transparency and accessibility of the consultation process and equal opportunity to participate. Assess whether the consultation explicitly documents mechanisms for submitting feedback (not merely that a portal exists elsewhere). Lack of explicit mention and limited channels can reduce score. Example: Draft Kerala IT Policy scored low because the policy did not mention feedback mechanisms despite a separate webpage accepting comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the consultation document was translated into relevant regional/national languages (and accessible formats like braille, sign-language transcriptions) appropriate to the target audience to ensure linguistic inclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises plain-language drafting in translations per OECD guidance. Jury deliberation led to a quantitative rule-of-thumb: for consultations with national scope, English and Hindi translations are expected; for regional scope, English plus at least one regional language. Accessibility supports meaningful participation in linguistically diverse contexts. Example: Draft Kerala IT Policy met expectations by providing English and Malayalam versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the consulting body provided a report, summary, or published the responses received (in part or entirety) after the consultation closed, demonstrating that public input was received and considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative criterion aligned with PLCP Section 6 which requires placement of summary of feedback/comments on the department website. Also draws on UNDP public consultation index guidance. Look for published summaries, datasets of comments, or descriptions of how feedback informed changes. Absence of post-consultation publication or summaries lowers score severely. Example: Draft Kerala IT Policy scored 1/5 for no published reports or public comments after the consultation period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the consulting body is responsive to communications (letters, RTIs, direct requests) from citizens or civic organisations—i.e., willing to address queries and share information after the consultation to reinforce trust and encourage future participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A qualitative higher-order criterion recommended by the jury to capture feedback loops beyond publication. Consider whether authorities answer information requests, share lists of comments received, and indicate whether/when final versions will be released. Note: in practice responsiveness was scored only for the final 26 nominees due to data-collection burdens. Example: Kerala government responded fully to an RTI and provided a list of comments, earning a high responsiveness score (4/5).
